name: Monzo
summary: Monzo explains its interviews on its own blog. For backend engineers it describes a recruiter call, an initial call, a take-home or pair-coding exercise, a systems design interview and a behavioural interview with two interviewers. In systems design it says it wants to hear your trade-offs, not neat diagrams, and in the behavioural round it wants to know which parts you led yourself. Data, machine learning and credit roles follow a similar shape with case studies or solution design in place of systems design.
rounds: Recruiter call: an introduction to Monzo and the process
Initial call with someone from the team
Take-home task or pair-coding exercise (engineering); a take-home or case study for data and credit roles
Systems or solution design interview, talking through a problem with an engineer
Behavioural interview, often about an hour with two interviewers
Decision, with Monzo saying it tells candidates the outcome and next steps
looks_for: Being clear about what you did versus what the team did
Clean, readable code in the practical task

questions.text: Tell me about a project you led from start to finish. Which decisions were yours?
covers: The goal and your role
Two or three decisions you made yourself
The outcome and what you'd change

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to deliver something with an unclear or changing scope.
covers: What was unclear and why
How you clarified or narrowed it
What you shipped and when

questions.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical approach.
covers: Both approaches and their trade-offs
How you discussed it and decided
What happened and how the relationship held up

questions.text: Tell me about a time something you built caused a problem for users. What did you do?
covers: What went wrong and how you found out
How you fixed it and kept people informed
What you changed so it wouldn't happen again

questions.text: How would you design a service that sends customers a notification for every card payment within seconds?
covers: Events from the card processor to a queue to the notification sender
Handling retries and duplicates so nobody gets two alerts
What you'd monitor and what happens when a provider is down

questions.text: How would you make a money transfer safe to retry if the network drops halfway?
covers: Idempotency keys and how they're stored
Making the operation atomic or compensating
How the client knows what really happened

questions.text: Walk me through the trade-offs between a few small services and one larger one for a new product.
covers: What you gain and pay for with each
Team size, deployment and data ownership
Which you'd pick here and why

questions.text: How would you spot unusual spending patterns that might mean a customer's card has been stolen?
covers: Signals: location, amount, merchant, timing
Rules first, then models, and the cost of false alarms
What the customer sees and how they confirm

questions.text: Talk me through the code you wrote for the take-home: what would you do differently in production?
covers: The design you chose and why
Tests, error handling and logging you'd add
What you'd simplify or split

questions.text: How do you explain a technical decision to someone in operations or customer support?
covers: Starting from what they need to do differently
Plain words and one example
How you check it landed

questions.text: Why do you want to work at Monzo?
covers: Something specific about Monzo's product or approach you value
How your experience fits the role
What you'd like to work on

questions.text: What would you want to learn in your first six months here?
covers: Skills or areas you want to grow
How you'd get there with the team
How it helps Monzo too

tips: Monzo's blog has a post on its process for many roles; read the one for yours before the recruiter call.
In systems design, explain your trade-offs out loud. Monzo says tidy diagrams earn no extra credit.
In the behavioural round, say 'I' for what you did and 'we' for the team, and be clear which is which.
Pick a non-trivial project for the behavioural round, with real decisions you can talk about in depth.
